content: Patients who presented at public health centers in Jakarta at the end of 2018 were part of a study examining HIV testing coverage. The data compared sites receiving joint technical assistance (TA) service delivery with those that did not. In Myanmar, the HIV epidemic varies significantly across geographical locations and behavioral risk profiles. Urban and semi-urban areas, as well as regions with high rates of injecting drug use, show a substantially higher HIV burden. For instance, HIV prevalence among people who inject drugs ranges from 6% to 47% in different areas of Myanmar. In Kachin State, heroin use has fueled dual epidemics of injecting drug use and HIV infection. Putao, a remote township in northern Kachin State, is particularly challenging to access for regular healthcare services, yet drug use remains high in this area. Many people who inject drugs in Putao face significant barriers to accessing harm reduction services, including HIV testing and counseling, antiretroviral therapy (ART), needle and syringe programs, condom distribution, and diagnosis and treatment for tuberculosis (TB), sexually transmitted infections (STIs), hepatitis B (HBV), and hepatitis C (HCV). Since late 2017, Medical Action Myanmar (MAM), with funding from USAID and the Global Fund, has implemented a harm reduction project in Putao. This initiative employs a community-based intervention strategy using mobile clinic teams and integrates with existing networks of malaria community health workers (CHWs). These CHWs, already established in remote villages, provide malaria diagnosis and treatment alongside basic healthcare. Under the new model, CHWs are trained and mobilized to deliver HIV-related services, including health education, referrals for HIV testing and counseling, needle and syringe exchange, and referrals for methadone maintenance therapy (MMT) and ART. CHWs’ homes have been adapted to function as harm reduction service hubs, equipped with automated needle and syringe supply boxes, disposal facilities for used needles, and educational materials. These CHWs are regularly trained and monitored by a MAM mobile team led by a medical doctor, which includes a counselor and a peer educator. During mobile team visits, HIV testing, counseling, basic healthcare, health education, and linkage to confirmatory HIV testing, ART, and MMT are provided. Before MAM’s intervention, people who inject drugs in Putao were largely hidden, with integrated bio-behavioral survey (IBBS) data identifying only 35 individuals. However, the new model has significantly expanded the reach of harm reduction services, engaging over 1,200 people who inject drugs within a short timeframe, with strong community acceptance and support. Approximately 900 individuals have been screened and treated for HIV, HBV, HCV, STIs, and TB. This community-based service delivery model, integrated through existing CHWs, has proven feasible for improving identification, care linkage, and reducing HIV transmission among people who inject drugs in rural Myanmar. Globally, TB remains a significant public health issue, with 7 million new cases annually, 3% of which occur among people living with HIV. In India, the 2018 TB report highlighted that while an equal number of TB patients seek care in the private sector, only 13% of those notified from the private sector are aware of their HIV status. To address this gap, PATH introduced the Patient Provider Service Agency (PPSA) to engage private providers in offering free TB diagnosis and treatment services aligned with national standards. However, a gap persisted in documenting HIV status among private-sector TB patients. To improve HIV case-finding and linkage to ART among these patients, PATH collaborated with the Mumbai District AIDS Control Society (MDACS) and Maharashtra State AIDS Control Society (MSACS) under the Challenge TB mechanism, funded by PEPFAR. Strategies included strengthening private providers’ capacity for HIV rapid testing, establishing formal agreements for data reporting and free HIV testing, and employing link counselors to facilitate referrals for TB/HIV co-infected patients to public sector HIV centers for confirmatory testing and ART initiation. Of 13,003 TB patients notified from private sector sites, 73% were tested for HIV, with 278 testing positive. Among newly detected HIV-positive patients, 87% were linked to care, and 97% of those were initiated on ART. In Kenya, despite progress toward the 90-90-90 targets, HIV testing and treatment among men remain challenging. Concurrently, the country faces rising rates of non-communicable diseases (NCDs), particularly cardiovascular disease (CVD). To address these twin epidemics, PEPFAR and AstraZeneca partnered with PATH to integrate hypertension (HTN) and HIV screening, diagnosis, and treatment in western Kenya. Mobile blood pressure and HIV testing services were offered in 51 locations targeting men aged 18-50 in informal workplaces and social venues. This approach modestly increased HIV testing uptake among men, with non-stigmatizing HTN services serving as an entry point for engagement. In Vietnam, Lighthouse, a community-based organization, began offering free community-based HIV testing in 2016 through trained lay testers. This initiative addressed barriers such as inconvenient testing hours, lack of LGBTQ-friendly services, and poor follow-up for positive cases. Lighthouse’s services include on-site testing, hotspot and community event testing, and self-test kits. On-site testing allows for rapid sexual health screening, while self-testing and community events expand outreach. Peer educators promote services through online and offline channels. In 2018, Lighthouse provided HIV testing to 1,259 LGBTQ individuals, with 68 confirmed positive cases, all of whom were referred to ART services. A pilot project in Vietnam, supported by WHO, assessed the feasibility of lay and self-testing approaches for HIV, HCV, and syphilis among key populations. Rapid diagnostic tests were used, and peer educators were trained to provide testing, counseling, and linkage to care. The pilot demonstrated that passionate peer educators could effectively deliver services, with data informing national policy and program development. However, access to HCV diagnosis and treatment remains limited due to the lack of coverage for hepatitis C medications under national health insurance.
